facts.text: I like the stockholm syndrome aspect to the worm becoming loyal to Jareth after being transformed by him.
I think both aspects of the human to worm and worm to servant can be true.
The worm had a close relationship of some sort with the proto-Sarah.
The worm either received the book from proto-Sarah after she succumbed to tragedy or provided her with key information to put into the book.
The worm entrusted proto-Sarah with the necessary secrets and power to overcome Jareth.
The worm had knowledge and stewardship in the book that only someone such as the worm might know.
The worm may have had a romantic interest in proto-Sarah.
The worm was initially responsible for guiding proto-Sarah into the labyrinth where she meets Jareth.
The worm had good intentions to help proto-Sarah with Jareth's magic.
The worm becomes jealous at Jareth's skill at seducing proto-Sarah.
The worm begins to demonstrate disloyalty to Jareth out of jealousy.
The worm ultimately causes harm to himself and to Sarah in the process.
The secrets and stewardship in the book are the worm's way of atoning for causing harm to the one he loved.
I think the worm's character would probably have a lot of self-doubt and anxiety when it comes to approaching Sarah.
The worm may be charming in one sense but unattractive and off putting due to lack of confidence and self-effacing nature.
Even when giving good advice, the worm hesitates.
The worm's doubt can plant seeds of doubt in Sarah that grow.
The cracks in the worm's character and integrity begin to propagate in response to stressors from the introduction of Jareth into the dynamic.
I proposed prototyping a series of 10 back-and-forth dialogue exchanges between human worm and proto-Sarah set in their first meeting in the real world.
Human worm has left the labyrinth realm to observe reality.
Human worm finds reality more ordinary and paradoxically interesting.
Human worm steps in to intervene when proto-Sarah is in the throws of mania and having an existential crisis about to injure himself.
Human worm intervenes in a compassionate and understanding way that only someone well acquainted with madness can summon.
I wanted the dialogue to start with the worm abruptly calling out to Sarah with the line "Oh, but don't do that!"
I proposed making Sarah less surprised to see the worm and more unphased by his sudden appearance.
Sarah is accustomed to seeing and feeling unexplainable things, having delusions and an inappropriate sense of invulnerability.
Sarah is fantasizing about death but somehow doesn't believe she even can die.
Sarah is manic and psychotic.
Sarah has an odd manner of speech.
